To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CD30, TNFRp75, and CD40 contain TRAF binding sites and that these binding sites can be used to predict which TRAFs will bind a particular TNFR.
CD30 and related receptors have TRAF-binding motifs that mediate signalling events.
the cytoplasmic tails of CD30, CD40 and TNFRp75 contain binding sites for TRAF1-3, and that the amino acid sequences in these receptors which bind TRAFs are highly homologous.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of TRAF binding sites in the CD30 receptor and the demonstration of the ability of TRAFs to bind to CD30 and other related receptors.
identifying the molecular effectors of CD30-mediated signalling.
the identification and characterization of the CD30 signalling pathways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CD30 cytoplasmic tail has the potential to interact with all three TRAF molecules.
the CD30 receptor has a unique intracellular tail which binds TRAF1,2, and 4 in a selective manner.
the amino acid sequence 576MLSVEEG583 of CD30 binds TRAF1, and the amino acid sequence, 558PHYPET565, binds both TRAF2 and TRAF3.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CD30 receptor binds TRAF1, and 2 and 3 and that the TRAF-binding sites are conserved in the CD30, TNFRp75, and CD40 molecules, and that these receptors can selectively bind TRAFs in the order of TRAF2, 3, and 1.
TRAF1,2 and 3 bind to the CD30, CD40, and TNFRp75 intracellular domains and that these TRAFs are the likely effectors for signalling events in these receptors.
CD30, TNFRp75, and CD40 have a common mechanism of TRAF binding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CD30, TNFRp75, and CD40 receptors share a common mechanism for signalling via TRAFs.
the CD30 cytoplasmic tail contains multiple TRAF binding sequences that can selectively interact with TRAF1,2, and 2.
the TRAF-binding sequences in CD30, TNFRp75, and CD40 are highly conserved, and the binding specificity is determined by a single amino acid residue within the motif.
